abstain

ab-STAYN -- the second syllable rhymes with 'rain'. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To abstain is to restrain oneself from doing or enjoying something.

The councilwoman chose to abstain from the vote because her family owned land near the proposed construction site.

Example

Dessert is passed around the table, but the marathon runner chooses to abstain, politely waving it away and sticking to the strict diet she follows before every race.

Deliberately holding herself back from something tempting is exactly what it means to abstain. Unlike 'indulge,' which means giving in to a desire, to abstain means to refuse it on purpose.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

forgo: To forgo something is to give it up or do without it, usually letting a particular chance or claim pass — you might forgo your turn or forgo a bonus. To abstain is firmer and more inward: deliberately holding yourself back from an indulgence itself, often for a long stretch.

forbear: To forbear is to hold yourself back with patient self-control, usually from a sharp word or rash act in the heat of a moment. To abstain is less about patience under provocation and more about denial: deliberately going without something you would enjoy.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

indulge: to give in to a desire or pleasure

partake: to take part in something or have a share of it

Where it sits · how firm and lasting the self-denial is

refrain → abstain → desist

refrain vs. abstain: Refrain is lighter and usually briefer than abstain — you refrain when you hold yourself back from starting something, like refraining from talking during a movie, while to abstain is a firmer, longer-lasting act of self-denial.

desist vs. abstain: Desist can sound stronger and more official than abstain: to abstain is a personal choice to hold back, while desist often means stopping something already underway, sometimes because an authority demands it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — abs-: away, away from (Latin)

root — tain: to hold (from Latin tenere; spelled -tain in English, as in retain and contain)

Put it together: Abstain comes from Latin abs- ('away from') plus tenere ('to hold'), spelled -tain in English. To abstain is literally to hold yourself away from something -- you keep your own hands off the thing you are refusing.

Use the root in a new word: retain: No one at the meeting would say whether the firm meant to retain its downtown office.

Root Check

Word Choice

Abstain is almost always followed by 'from,' as in 'abstain from sweets' or 'abstain from arguing.' It is also the official word for choosing not to cast a vote at all -- a determined act of self-restraint rather than simple forgetfulness.
